# The Meeting Is Not the Work

Most bad meetings aren't bad because the people in them are bad at meetings. They're bad because nobody decided what the meeting was *for*, and so it defaulted to the only thing a group of people can do without a purpose: talk until the calendar says stop.

Here's how to do better. Not with a new tool or a novelty timer, but with a handful of decisions you make before anyone walks in the room.

## Start by not having the meeting

The highest-leverage meeting improvement is deletion. Before you send an invite, ask what you actually need:

- **Sharing information?** Write it down. A document can be read at 3x the speed of speech, skimmed, searched, and referenced six months later. A status meeting is a document being read aloud badly.
- **Gathering input?** A well-framed async request often gets you better thinking, because people can respond after considering rather than performing in real time.
- **Making a decision, resolving a disagreement, or building shared understanding of something genuinely ambiguous?** Now you have a meeting.

The rough test: if the value comes from the *interaction* — people building on each other, hearing tone, arguing, reading the room — meet. If the value is in the *content*, write.

This also applies to meetings that already exist. Look at your recurring invites. Every one of them was created to solve a problem that may or may not still exist. Give them expiration dates. "This weekly sync ends in eight weeks unless we actively renew it" is a sentence that will save you dozens of hours a year.

## Write the agenda as questions, not topics

Here is a topic: "Q3 roadmap."

Here is a question: "Do we cut the reporting feature to ship onboarding by September 15, or do we move the date?"

The topic agenda produces a meandering discussion where everyone says something about the roadmap and then time runs out. The question agenda produces an answer.

Every agenda item should be phrased as a question to answer or a decision to make, with an owner and a time budget. If you can't write the question, you don't understand what you want yet — and that's useful information. Go figure it out before you spend eight people's hour.

A good agenda looks like:

> **1. (10 min, Priya) Do we ship onboarding without the reporting feature?** Decision. Context in the doc below.
> **2. (15 min, Marcus) What's causing the support ticket spike?** Diagnosis — we need to leave with a hypothesis and an owner.
> **3. (5 min, all) What did we miss?**

Note the third item. Leaving a small slot for "what did we miss" catches the thing that would otherwise derail item one.

## Name the decider before you start

Most meetings that feel endless are meetings where nobody knows who decides. So the group circles, seeking a consensus that isn't coming, until someone with authority gets impatient and unilaterally ends it — which teaches everyone that the previous forty minutes were theater.

Say it out loud at the top: "Priya owns this call. We're here to give her the best possible input, and then she decides." This is not authoritarian. It's the opposite — it makes the input phase real, because everyone knows exactly what it's for and when it closes.

Consensus is a beautiful thing when it happens naturally and an enormous tax when you chase it. Aim for *consent* — people can live with the decision — not agreement.

## Invite fewer people

Every additional attendee costs more than their hour. Groups get slower and more cautious as they grow; people perform for the audience; someone always feels obligated to justify their presence with a comment.

Give everyone a reason to be there: they're deciding, they have information nobody else has, they're doing the work that results, or they need context they genuinely can't get from the notes. "Might be interested" is not a reason. Send them the notes.

If someone's only needed for one item, invite them for that item and let them go. It feels awkward the first time and then it feels obviously correct.

The generous version of this: make it explicitly safe to decline. "Optional for you — I'll send notes" is a gift. So is a culture where people can leave a meeting that turned out not to need them.

## Steal the silent read

If you have a pre-read, do not assume it's been read. It hasn't. People are busy and hope for the best.

The fix, borrowed from Amazon and worth the borrowing: spend the first five to ten minutes of the meeting reading the document, in silence, together. It feels strange for about ninety seconds and then it feels like the most efficient thing you've ever done. Everyone arrives at the discussion with the same context at the same moment. Nobody has to sit through a fifteen-minute verbal recap of something they already read.

Have people comment directly in the doc while they read. By the time the discussion starts, you can see where the disagreement is and go straight there.

## Facilitate, and know that facilitating is a job

The person running the meeting is doing real work: watching the clock, noticing who hasn't spoken, catching when the conversation has stopped producing new information, deciding when to cut something off.

That job is hard to do while also being the most opinionated person in the room. If you're the senior person, consider handing facilitation to someone else — partly for bandwidth, mostly because your opinions will otherwise land like verdicts and end the discussion early.

Some facilitation moves worth having in your pocket:

- **"Let's hear from people who haven't spoken."** The simplest airtime fix there is.
- **"Before we discuss — everyone take two minutes and write your answer down."** Independent thinking before group thinking. Prevents the first speaker from anchoring everyone else, and it's a huge equalizer for people who don't think out loud.
- **"That's a good question and it's not this meeting."** Then write it on the parking lot list, visibly, so the person knows it wasn't discarded.
- **"I want to make sure I understand the disagreement. Sam, you think X because Y. Dana, you think not-X because Z. Is that right?"** Half the time, naming the crux dissolves it. The other half, at least you're arguing about the right thing.
- **"We've got ten minutes left and one decision to make."** Say it before the last minute, not during.

## The last five minutes are the most valuable

The most common way a good meeting produces nothing is that it ends with a warm collective feeling and no record of what happened.

Reserve the final few minutes. Out loud, and in writing, capture:

- **What we decided** (and what we explicitly deferred)
- **Who is doing what by when** — a name and a date, not "the team" and "soon"
- **Who else needs to know**

Read it back before people leave. This is when you discover that two people heard the decision differently, which is much cheaper to find out now than in three weeks.

Send the notes the same day. Short is fine — decisions and owners is enough. The notes are the artifact; the meeting was just how you made them.

## Start on time and end early

Start at the start time. Do not recap for latecomers — it punishes the punctual and rewards the opposite, and people notice which one you're doing.

And when the work is done, end. A meeting scheduled for an hour that finishes in thirty-five minutes has not failed at anything. Giving people back twenty-five minutes is a real gift, and it builds a reputation that means people will actually show up to your next one.

While you're at it: schedule 25 and 50 minutes instead of 30 and 60. Humans need to walk somewhere, refill something, and think for a moment. Back-to-back-to-back calendars produce people who are physically present and cognitively still in the last meeting.

## The underlying idea

Every one of these practices comes from the same place: **a meeting is an expensive, synchronous, hard-to-reverse use of other people's attention, and it should be treated that way.**

You don't need to run meetings perfectly. You just need to be the person who has clearly thought about why everyone is there. That alone puts you in a small minority, and people will notice — usually by saying something like "that was actually a good meeting," in a tone of mild surprise.

Take the compliment. Then look at your calendar and see what else you can delete.

# Meeting Hygiene, Second Pass

You know the playbook. Agenda as questions. Named decider. Silent read at the top. Fewer people, same-day notes, kill the recurring meetings nobody remembers creating. You may have written some of it yourself in a Notion doc that three people read.

And your calendar is still bad.

That's not an execution problem, and one more listicle won't fix it. The standard advice is correct and insufficient, because it treats meetings as a coordination technology when they're mostly a political and emotional one. Here's the version for people who already tried the first version.

## Every persistent bad meeting is solving a problem you haven't named

If a meeting is obviously useless and it still exists, it isn't useless. It's doing something other than its stated job, and whatever that something is, it's load-bearing.

The usual suspects:

**Anxiety management.** A weekly status meeting where nothing happens is often a VP's way of confirming the building hasn't burned down. The information is in the dashboard, but the dashboard doesn't produce the feeling. Delete the meeting and the anxiety reroutes into Slack DMs, which is worse.

**Diffusion of responsibility.** Some meetings exist so that a decision has eleven witnesses. Nobody wants to own the call, so they manufacture a room where the call gets made ambiently and no single name is attached. These meetings are exquisitely resistant to your DACI framework, because clarity is the thing they're designed to prevent.

**Access.** For a lot of people, the weekly sync is the only reliable channel to someone senior. Cancel it and you haven't saved their time — you've cut off their escalation path, and they will find a more expensive way to escalate.

**Belonging.** The meeting is where people find out they're still on the team.

You cannot delete a meeting by attacking its stated purpose. You have to substitute for its real one. Replace the status meeting with a written update *plus* a standing 15-minute slot the anxious VP can use whenever they want, and it'll actually stick. Skip the substitution and the meeting comes back in ninety days under a new name.

So before you kill anything: what breaks, and for whom, and what do they do instead?

## Async isn't the default; convergence pressure is the variable

"Could this have been an email" is a slogan, not an analysis. Written communication has real costs that async-maximalists systematically underweight:

- **Latency compounds.** A decision requiring four exchanges takes four days async and eleven minutes live. Sometimes the eleven minutes is cheap at the price.
- **It advantages writers.** Async-first cultures quietly hand disproportionate influence to whoever writes fastest and most confidently, which correlates with fluency and seniority more than with being right.
- **Threads fork.** Disagreement in a comment thread branches instead of converging. Nobody has to concede in writing, so nobody does.
- **It's bad at conflict.** Text strips tone, and people read hostility into neutral sentences. Any exchange with real disagreement in it degrades in writing.

The useful variable isn't sync-vs-async. It's whether the thing needs **convergence pressure** — a moment where the group must actually land somewhere, with social cost attached to not landing. Meetings manufacture convergence pressure. That's their comparative advantage, and it's nearly the only one.

So: information distribution, async. Idea generation, async (groups are worse at it live anyway). Anything requiring a group to *converge under disagreement* — meet, and know that's what you're paying for.

## Whoever frames the question has already won

"Write the agenda as a question, not a topic" is good advice that quietly hands you a lot of power, and you should be honest with yourself about using it.

"Do we cut reporting to ship onboarding by the 15th?" has smuggled in the premise that those are the two options. Someone in that room thinks the real question is whether onboarding should ship at all, and now they have to fight the agenda before they can fight the substance — which reads as obstruction and costs them credibility.

The framing *is* the decision, most of the time. Two implications:

If you're framing: circulate the question before the meeting to the people most likely to disagree with it, specifically asking whether it's the right question. This is not politeness. It's the cheapest possible way to find out that your entire agenda is built on a premise your staff engineer thinks is insane.

If you're attending: contest the frame in the first two minutes or accept it. Litigating the question at minute forty makes you the person who derailed the meeting, regardless of whether you were right.

## The decider is whoever can reopen it

Naming a decider fails constantly, and it fails in a specific way: you name the nominal decider, and there's someone else who can quietly reverse the decision later without ever having been in the room.

The diagnostic is simple. Ask: **who can reopen this, and what would it take?**

If the answer is "the CTO, in a hallway, in about four seconds," then you didn't run a decision meeting. You ran a recommendation meeting. That's fine — recommendation meetings are legitimate and useful — but calling it a decision meeting is a lie the room can detect, and it produces the specific cynicism where people stop bringing real objections because they know the real conversation happens somewhere else.

Say what it is. "We're producing a recommendation for Dana, who'll take it Thursday. Our job is to make it good enough that she says yes." People engage seriously with an honest recommendation meeting. They perform at a dishonest decision meeting.

Related: if a decision keeps getting reopened, the problem is almost never the meeting. It's that the decision was made without someone whose consent it actually needed, and they're routing around it. Adding a decision-log entry won't help. Finding that person will.

## Attendance is a status good, so meetings accrete

Calendars grow because inclusion is a signal and exclusion is an insult. Nobody gets promoted for declining. The cost of one more attendee is diffuse and the cost of leaving someone out is specific and personal, so the gradient points one direction forever.

You can't fix this with individual willpower. You need structure that makes shrinkage the default:

- **Expiration dates on recurring meetings.** Not "we'll review it," which never happens — an actual end date, requiring an actual renewal. Most won't get renewed, and nobody has to be the person who killed anything.
- **Periodic bankruptcy.** Once a year, delete every recurring meeting on the team and let people re-create only what they miss. You'll re-create maybe half. This is brutal and it works, and it works partly *because* it's indiscriminate — no one's meeting was singled out.
- **Separate attendance from access.** The reason people fight to stay on invites is that the invite is how they find out what happened. Make notes genuinely good and genuinely public, and the invite stops being the only channel. Most of the resistance to being uninvited is actually resistance to being uninformed.

## You can only set defaults

Past a certain scope you cannot facilitate your way to better meetings, because you're not in most of them. What propagates isn't skill, it's defaults: calendar lengths, template agendas, whether declining is normal, whether people watch you leave meetings that turned out not to need you.

Most of the leverage is in a handful of dumb, mechanical things that survive without a skilled human in the room. Default event length set to 25 minutes. A meeting template that won't let you save without a question and an owner. A norm that anyone can ask "what are we deciding?" without it being rude. A decision log that's actually maintained.

The decision log is the underrated one. Meetings are ephemeral and decisions decay — six months out, nobody remembers what was decided or why, so it gets relitigated by people who weren't there. A searchable record of *decision, date, rationale, who decided* eliminates an entire category of meeting: the one where you rebuild context that was never written down.
